transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

Yeah, hi. Thanks for seeing me. I, uh, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten... well, they've always been a bit chaotic, to be honest, but lately, it's just become completely untenable. I'm a software developer, and I've got a graduate degree, so you'd think I'd have a system for this stuff by now at my age, but I just... what finally pushed me to come in is that I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. 

And there are just so many moving parts right now. Just to give you an idea of what my desk looks like on any given day, I've got these incredibly dense patent notes I need to review for a new piece of software we're trying to protect. At the exact same time, I'm supposed to be doing all this workshop prep—which I volunteered to lead months ago thinking it would be fine, but now the date is right on top of me. Plus, I'm dealing with these strict gallery deadlines for a digital art installation I'm doing on the side, and on top of all of that, I have to make a dozen little team decisions every day at my actual job. 

It's like this massive tangled web in my head. And instead of sitting down and figuring out what the actual priority is, or, you know, making a logical schedule and tackling the most important thing first, I just... I end up starting whatever is loudest. You know what I mean? Like, whatever is pinging me on Slack right that second, or whichever deadline is literally screaming in my face, that's what I do. I just react to the noise instead of doing what actually matters. The patent notes are crucial, they're incredibly important, but because the lawyer isn't actively yelling at me today, they just sit there gathering dust while I spend three hours tweaking a slide for the workshop just because I happened to open that file first. It's exhausting, and I just can't keep operating this way.
Can you tell me how you've been feeling emotionally lately, especially when you're not caught up in all the tasks and deadlines?

Emotionally? Uh, geez. That’s... I mean, I’m not really sure how to answer that, to be perfectly honest with you. Because the premise of the question—when I’m *not* caught up in the tasks and deadlines—it almost feels like a completely hypothetical scenario at this point in my life. 

Like, if you're asking if I'm walking around feeling profoundly sad all the time, or, I don't know, crying in my car, or having some kind of major emotional mood swings... no. I haven't noticed anything like that at all. I don't really have any overarching emotional... things... going on, as far as I can tell. 

I mean, my wife and I were actually just talking about something similar over the weekend. We were sitting out on the patio, and I had promised her I would leave my phone inside for at least an hour so we could just have a normal Sunday morning coffee. Which is this whole ritual we used to be really good about, you know, grinding the beans fresh and just sitting together, but lately it has completely fallen by the wayside. Anyway, sitting there, emotionally, I felt... fine? I guess? I wasn't depressed or angry or anything. 

But the thing is, even when I'm physically removed from the desk and trying to just be a person drinking coffee, my brain is still running the tape of all the things I'm dropping the ball on. I'm sitting there looking at the yard, but in my head, I'm drafting an apology email to the gallery curator. So I don't really know if I even *have* a distinct emotional state outside of all the work right now, because the work is always just sort of hovering there in the background. So, yeah, emotionally... I really don't think there's anything specific to report. I don't know. I'm just sort of normal, I guess, just buried underneath all the logistical chaos.
Have you noticed any loss of interest or pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy, even when you're not thinking about work or deadlines?

No, no, not at all. It's actually... well, if anything, it’s almost the exact opposite. I still have a ton of interest in the things I like doing. When I actually get to do them, I enjoy them just as much as I ever did. 

Like, for example, I have this hobby where I restore vintage mechanical keyboards. I know, it’s a massive cliché for a software developer in his forties to be obsessed with old clicky keyboards, but I’ve been doing it for over a decade. I source these old, broken boards from the eighties and nineties off eBay, and I take them completely apart, clean the switches, resolder the connections, retrobright the plastic cases—the whole nine yards. And when I’m out in the garage at my workbench doing that? I love it. I genuinely love it. I get completely absorbed in the tactile nature of it, figuring out why a particular key isn't registering or tracking down a specific replacement spring. It’s incredibly satisfying to me. 

So the pleasure is absolutely still there. The spark hasn't gone out for that, or for the digital art I mentioned, or, you know, just going out to try a new restaurant with my wife. I still really want to do all of it. The issue is more that... I just can't seem to find the space to do those things properly, or if I do, I'm doing them at the expense of something I was supposed to be finishing. 

Like, I'll sit down to just quickly test a switch on an old IBM Model M board, having a great time, and then suddenly realize three hours have completely vanished and I never even opened those patent notes I was supposed to read. So the fun things often just become another vehicle for me to avoid the work, which then leads to this massive wave of guilt. But the actual, fundamental enjoyment of the activity itself? No, I haven't lost that at all. If anything, I’m constantly craving those hobbies because they feel so much better and more manageable than the chaotic mess of my actual responsibilities. So, yeah, to answer your question, no loss of interest whatsoever. I just wish I could enjoy them without the baggage of everything else I'm failing to do.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried about not being able to keep up with your responsibilities, even when you know logically that you're doing your best?

Anxious or worried... uh, hmm. No, actually. I don't think so. I mean, it’s a totally fair question, given everything I just dumped on you about the deadlines and the chaos, but... no. I don’t think I’d use the word anxious. 

Because, well, to address the second half of what you just said—the part about knowing logically that I’m doing my best—that’s actually the crux of it right there. I *don’t* think I’m doing my best. If I were actually sitting down, putting in a solid eight or nine hours of focused work, and still falling behind just because the sheer volume of the workload was humanly impossible, then yeah, I could see myself being incredibly anxious or worried about failing. But I know I’m *not* doing my best. I know perfectly well that I spent three hours yesterday looking at custom resin keycaps on Reddit instead of reviewing the software architecture document my team desperately needs by Friday. So it’s not really worry or anxiety about my capacity to keep up, because I know exactly why I’m not keeping up. It’s me. I'm the bottleneck.

So, no, I don’t really get anxious. I don’t have that feeling of dread or, you know, a tight chest, or racing thoughts about the future. It’s more just... a profound annoyance with myself? Like, I’ll be sitting there, fully aware of the consequences of not doing the thing, and I just don't do it. But I definitely wouldn't call that anxiety. 

I actually used to work with a guy, Dave—great guy, brilliant back-end developer, we were at a startup together back in 2015—and he had actual, severe anxiety. He would literally make himself physically sick worrying about deployment days. He'd be completely paralyzed by all the "what ifs," sweating, pacing the floor, terrified the servers were going to crash. I don’t have any of that. I’m not sitting around worried about "what if the code breaks" or "what if the gallery curator hates my installation." I know the code is solid, and I know the art is good. The only "what if" in my life is "what if I just never get around to actually hitting send on the email." 

So, yeah, no anxiety or worry per se. I'm not sitting up at night wringing my hands over it. It's just this constant, low-level frustration that I can't seem to just operate like a normal professional adult who gets things done on a normal timeline.

Can you recall if this pattern of difficulty staying on task, prioritizing, and following through on responsibilities has been a long-standing issue for you, even going back to your school days or earlier in your career?

Oh, wow. Yeah. Long-standing doesn't even begin to cover it. I mean, it definitely was an issue early in my career—I could tell you stories about my first junior dev job where I almost got fired for missing a massive code freeze—but if I really think about it, if I'm being completely honest, this goes back way, way further than that. 

Looking back, this was absolutely there in grade school too. I actually know this for a fact because my mom is one of those people who kept absolutely everything. Every macaroni art project, every spelling test, you name it. A few years ago, my wife and I were helping my parents clear out their house to downsize into a condo, and we found this massive plastic storage bin in the attic just full of my old school stuff. I sat down and started reading through my old report cards, and it was honestly like reading a script that had been written about my life. 

Every single one of them, year after year, had the exact same comments written in the margins by the teachers. They all wrote that I was bright, or that I had "so much potential," but that I constantly daydreamed. I’d just be staring out the window or taking apart my pens instead of listening. And the follow-through was just non-existent. I would literally do the work—I’d sit at the kitchen table, finish the math worksheet, and pack it up—but then I completely forgot to turn in the finished assignments the next day. It was like the bridge between doing the work and actually handing it to the teacher just didn't exist in my brain. 

And the organization... geez. I lost homework folders constantly. I went through so many of those neon pocket folders because they would just vanish. I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mr. Henderson, actually made me dump out my entire desk onto the classroom floor once because I swore I had my history worksheet, and it was just this embarrassing avalanche of crumpled papers, broken pencils, and permission slips from three months prior. 

So, yeah, this was all happening long before I was a teenager. It’s not a new pattern at all. It’s just... back then, the consequences were missing recess or getting a C-minus on a geography quiz, and now the consequences are letting down my entire development team or ruining a gallery showing. But the underlying mechanism? The inability to just track a task from point A to point B without getting completely derailed? Yeah, it's exactly the same. It’s always been like this.
